title: Hally’s
intro: A neighbourhood café rebrand built around a tangle of moments.

blocks.caption: Contemporary exterior image study / AI-assisted motion

blocks.label: The challenge
blocks.body: A neighbourhood café in Parsons Green needed an identity that felt as welcoming, energetic and distinctive as the place its regulars already knew.

blocks.label: The approach
blocks.body: A café is a place where lives briefly cross. A wandering, looping line connects those moments across illustration, menus, packaging and the website. The refinement of the typography gives the loose hand-drawn line something to push against.

blocks.label: The illustrations
blocks.body: A hand-drawn collection of glassware, food and small observations gives the wandering line a cast of characters.

title: Sussex
intro: A wordmark built from a county flag, for the Gladwin Brothers' flagship wine bar and restaurant.

sources.label: Jason’s published Random Order project — captured 12 November 2026

blocks.label: The Challenge
body: Sussex needed to feel distinct from the Gladwin Brothers' six other London restaurants — refined, intentional, and rooted in a specific place, not just another wine bar.

blocks.label: The Approach
body: The solution came from a detail most people never notice: Sussex is the only English county whose flag carries six golden martlets in a triangular formation. Rather than design a conventional logo, we let the name itself take that shape — SUSSEX set across three lines in a triangular grid mirroring the flag, the X anchoring the composition like a keystone. The system flexes: six coffee beans for takeaway, six wine droplets for the wine list, six wildflowers for seasonal menus — same rhythm, shifting tone.

blocks.label: The System, Flexing
body: The same grid flexes across contexts: six martlets for the core mark, six coffee beans for takeaway, six wine droplets for the wine list, six wildflowers for seasonal menus. Same rhythm, shifting tone.

blocks.quote: "Now, with six thriving restaurants across London, Jason's unparalleled creativity and vision have been essential at every turn."

blocks.label: Posters
body: Each event poster subtly references the six martlets of the Sussex flag through a triangular arrangement — six small plates for Tapas Night, six glass silhouettes for Cocktail Hour, six abstract forms for the gallery event. Quiet continuity across the campaign, with room to vary.

blocks.label: Colours
body: A palette built around the region itself — the deep tonal qualities of the South Downs, balanced against an unexpected breath of spring.

title: BSTN × Sneaker LAB

blocks.label: Thinking Unity
blocks.body: Thinking Unity. Rather than placing two identities side by side, the concept finds common ground in the culture surrounding the product. The basketball court provides the organising idea: a graphic language of lines, rhythm, movement and connection.

title: Superbalist
intro: Six years. One evolving digital ecosystem. From identity to interface, from components to systems.

metadata.label: Scope
metadata.value: Product design / UX / Identity / Stitch design system

blocks.label: Six years in the making
blocks.body: Superbalist was never simply about designing screens. It was about creating coherence across an increasingly complex world of fashion, technology, commerce and human interaction.

blocks.title: From the S to a shared design language.

blocks.label: Designing the system
blocks.body: At the centre of the visual language was the S. A recognisable symbol extending into a broader vocabulary of shapes, icons and digital expressions. Identity was not simply applied to the product; it became part of how the product communicated. As the platform evolved, Stitch brought structure to complexity: typography, grids, colour, components and interaction patterns formed a shared design language. The objective was not uniformity, but a system flexible enough to evolve without losing its identity.

blocks.label: Six years of evolution
blocks.body: Designing a digital product over six years changes your perspective. Individual screens become journeys. Components become systems. Small decisions accumulate into an experience used by real people. The work was never finished. It evolved with the technology, the business and the people using it.

blocks.label: Revisiting the work
blocks.body: Years later, I have returned to this body of work through a different creative lens. Using contemporary generative tools, I have begun reconstructing and reinterpreting elements of my original interface designs, iconography and visual systems. These new images are not historical screenshots. They are contemporary visual studies grounded in the original design thinking — a way of revisiting six years of work as an evolving design language.

blocks.label: Source artefacts
blocks.body: The source material brings interface structure and visual language together: order tracking, delivery states, icon construction, mobile composition and the principles behind Stitch. These archive artefacts sit alongside the contemporary reconstructions above.

title: Wright Architects
intro: A wordmark built on a single precise cut — an identity as considered as the practice it belongs to.

blocks.label: The Challenge
body: Wright Architects needed a mark that could sit on a waterfront office front, a business card, and a set of drawings alike, and read as exactly what the practice is: precise, considered, unshowy. Nothing about it could look decorative — every line had to earn its place. I worked alongside creative director Warren van Rensburg , who helped shape the brand's positioning, strategy, and creative direction.

blocks.label: The Approach
body: The whole identity turns on a single decision: every terminal in the wordmark is cut at exactly 17.5°, the same angle, repeated without exception. Set it against a straight edge and the cut all but disappears — subtle enough that most people will never consciously clock it. Soften those terminals back to a plain 90°, though, and the mark goes flat: it loses the quiet tension that makes it read as drawn, not typed. That's "surgical precision" in one detail — a cut small enough to go unnoticed, essential enough to hold the whole structure together. The kind of exactness a good architect works in without ever pointing at it.

blocks.label: The Outcome
body: The same 17.5° geometry carries the identity across the whole practice — signage, business cards, letterhead — without a single additional flourish. A mark built on restraint, for a practice that trades on the same.

blocks.label: Client
body: Greg Wright, Director, Wright Architects

sources.label: Jason’s published Random Order project — captured 12 November 2026

title: Scott USA
intro: A global art collaboration, passed from artist to artist across continents — one canvas, one long story.

blocks.label: The Brief
body: Scott USA had a wild idea for their snowboarding products: a global art collaboration that felt like a creative chain letter, passing one canvas from artist to artist across continents, each adding their own piece to the story.

blocks.label: The Approach
body: When the canvas reached South Africa, I was the third artist to contribute — the only one chosen from the entire African continent, which meant a great deal. I painted a fisherman, fitting for a canvas that had already crossed an ocean with a long journey still ahead. At the time I went by "Further," a nod to Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters' bus, worked into the piece as both signature and a marker of the distance between each artist involved. That piece became the hero image on the final packaging and t-shirt design.

blocks.quote: "Working with Jason is an excellent experience. He is a talented, hard-working professional that is passionate about his craft."

blocks.label: The Outcome
body: A surreal, proud moment: a painting born from a single South African contribution to a global chain, ending up as the face of the product itself.

blocks.label: Client
body: Nowel Pawliw, Art Director, Scott USA

title: G Adventures
intro: A custom illustration and icon system for a travel company running over 700 itineraries in more than 100 countries.

blocks.label: The Brief
body: G Adventures specializes in guided tours for small groups, tailoring travel packages to each traveler's preferences — they even collaborate with National Geographic on some trips. To stand out in a market crowded with photography, we decided to lead with custom illustration instead.

blocks.label: The Approach
body: Working with G Adventures' upper management, we developed a unique graphic style built to scale across the site — header postcards for each region of the world, and a full icon set covering everything from booking status to trip type. Same linework, same warmth, wherever a traveler lands on the site.

blocks.label: Header Postcards
body: A postcard illustration for every region G Adventures operates in — each one distinct, all of them clearly part of the same family.

blocks.label: The Icon Set
body: A full library covering booking status, trip type, and traveler preference — small enough to sit next to a line of copy, distinctive enough to carry the brand on their own.

blocks.quote: "Illustrations played an important part of the project and we were thrilled with the results. Jason was collaborative, and went above and beyond with a fresh perspective that made the results even better."

blocks.label: Trees for Life
body: The same illustration language extended to G Adventures' sustainability initiatives — giving the environmental side of the business the same warmth as the trip-planning side.

blocks.label: The Outcome
body: A cohesive illustration system now carries G Adventures across the entire site — recognisable at a glance, warm at every touchpoint, built to grow as new destinations and features are added.

blocks.label: Client
body: Greg Cormier, VP Digital & E-Commerce, G Adventures

title: Selected Brandmarks
intro: Behind every simple logo is a not-so-simple idea. A look behind the curtain at how these marks came to life.

blocks.label: About the Process
body: The marks here are rooted in strategy, story, and reduction — a balance between clarity and meaning. Each logo begins as a thought experiment: how do you express the soul of a brand using as little as possible? The answer often lives in dualities — function and feeling, concept and form.

blocks.label: The Backstory
body: Every logo starts with listening — getting close to a brand's personality, its ambitions, the people behind it. From there it's distillation: references, sketches, metaphors, patterns that feel both familiar and surprising. More often than not, the solution arrives when two distinct ideas lock together. That's where the spark is. That's where the logo begins.

blocks.label: Tortuga Loca — Mexican Radiance
body: For this bold, vibrant Mexican kitchen, the logo brings together symbolism from faith and folklore. A sharp monogram "T" radiates outward from a hexagonal frame — the hexagon a nod to a tortoise-shell plate, the radiant lines borrowed from the iconography of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Grounded and glowing, at once.
Our Lady of Guadalupe
Tortoise Shell
Tortuga Loca

blocks.label: Wilma — Caring First
body: Wilma supports people through the challenging days after losing a loved one, making estate transfers clearer and easier. Rounded letterforms and a small heart hidden in the "m" convey warmth — modern, comforting, and quietly optimistic, unlike the neutral tones common in the industry.

blocks.label: Good Luck — Bottled Goodness
body: This bottled citrus brand brings together grapefruit, blood orange, and lime. The wordmark divides into eight even segments — the natural geometry of citrus cut crosswise, and the brand's core values: simple, and full of character.

blocks.label: Outlier Health — Eternal Balance
body: Balance sits at the heart of Outlier Medicine, a practice rooted in Eastern tradition. The logo draws from the yin-yang symbol, reinterpreted within a single letter — the "O" — transforming the brand's initial into a quiet symbol of equilibrium.

blocks.quote: Some logos tell you everything in a glance.

blocks.label: The Shed — Farm to Fork
body: For The Shed, a farm-to-fork restaurant, the usual knife and fork symbol became a gardener's fork and trowel — tools of the soil instead of the kitchen. A quiet visual shift that reframes the whole experience: great food starts in the ground.

blocks.label: The Outcome
body: Five brands, five different problems — the same process underneath each one: listen first, reduce until only the idea is left, then shape it into a mark that feels inevitable.
